whoa.headline: A day on Venus is longer than its year
whoa.summary: Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes longer than one trip around the Sun. Sunrise there is a rare event.
whoa.try: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.
whoa.tryLine: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.

whoa.headline: A straw works because of air, not magic suck
whoa.summary: You lower the pressure in your mouth. Outside air pushes the drink up the straw. Space has no air push, so straws fail there.
whoa.try: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.
whoa.tryLine: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.

whoa.headline: She spotted a supernova at 14
whoa.summary: Caroline Moore was 14 when she found an exploding star in another galaxy. She used a backyard-style telescope network and careful checking. Pro astronomers confirmed it.
whoa.try: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.
whoa.tryLine: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.

whoa.headline: Fold a T-shirt in two seconds
whoa.summary: Pinch the shoulder and the mid-chest, flip it over the other shoulder, then fold. Once you have the pinch points, it looks like a trick.
whoa.try: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.
whoa.tryLine: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.

whoa.headline: You interrupted and the room went quiet
whoa.summary: Own it fast: 'Sorry - finish your bit.' Then wait. That one line turns an oops into respect.
whoa.try: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.
whoa.tryLine: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.

whoa.headline: Penguins propose with a pebble
whoa.summary: Some penguins hunt for a smooth pebble and drop it at a partner's feet. If the pebble is accepted, that is a yes. Romance, but rocky.
whoa.try: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.
whoa.tryLine: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.

whoa.headline: Your body makes a new skeleton every 10 years
whoa.summary: Bone is not a dead stick. Cells nibble old bone and lay new bone. The skeleton you have at 20 is not the same material you had at 10.
whoa.try: Jump. That's the system answering back.
whoa.tryLine: Jump. That's the system answering back.

whoa.headline: Learn one useful knot: the bowline
whoa.summary: The bowline makes a loop that does not slip. Boats, trees, and rescue lines use it. Rabbit out the hole, around the tree, back down.
whoa.try: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.
whoa.tryLine: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.

whoa.headline: He built a Braille printer from Lego
whoa.summary: Shubham Banerjee was 13 when he made a cheap Braille printer using Lego Mindstorms so more kids could afford books they can feel.
whoa.try: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?
whoa.tryLine: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?

whoa.headline: Velcro is a burr that said yes
whoa.summary: A Swiss engineer pulled burrs off his dog and looked under a microscope. Tiny hooks. He copied them. Your trainers are wearing a plant idea.
whoa.try: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.
whoa.tryLine: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.

whoa.headline: Someone is left out at lunch
whoa.summary: You do not need a speech. 'Want to sit with us?' is enough. If they say no, you still planted a door.
whoa.try: Use it once this week. One sentence.
whoa.tryLine: Use it once this week. One sentence.

whoa.headline: A teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh a mountain
whoa.summary: The leftover core of a giant star is packed past imagining. A spoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes. Gravity won that argument.
whoa.try: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.

whoa.headline: An octopus has three hearts
whoa.summary: Two hearts pump blood to the gills. The third pumps blood to the rest of the body - and it actually stops when the octopus swims.
whoa.try: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?
whoa.tryLine: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?

whoa.headline: Planes don't float. They steal lift from air.
whoa.summary: The wing is curved so air on top moves faster and pushes less. Air underneath pushes more, and that extra push is lift. Same idea as holding your hand out a car window.
whoa.try: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.
whoa.tryLine: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.

whoa.headline: A 14-year-old built a windmill from scrap
whoa.summary: William Kamkwamba's village in Malawi had almost no electricity. He used a library book, a broken bicycle, and junkyard parts. The windmill lit his house and pumped water.
whoa.try: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?
whoa.tryLine: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?

whoa.headline: Tell if an egg is still good in 5 seconds
whoa.summary: Drop it in a glass of water. Fresh eggs sink and lie on their side. Old eggs stand up. Bad eggs float - throw those away.
whoa.try: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.
whoa.tryLine: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.

whoa.headline: Your friend got the part you wanted
whoa.summary: First feeling: unfair. Good move: "Congrats. You earned it." Then ask the teacher what to practise for next time. You look strong, and you get a plan.
whoa.try: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.
whoa.tryLine: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.

whoa.headline: You cannot tickle yourself. Your brain blocks you.
whoa.summary: Your brain predicts your own fingers, so the surprise is gone. Tickling needs a tiny "I didn't see that coming." That's why another person works and you don't.
whoa.try: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.
whoa.tryLine: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.

whoa.headline: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the sun
whoa.summary: The sun's surface is about 5,500°C. A lightning bolt can hit 30,000°C. That's why it turns air into a flash and a boom you hear later.
whoa.try: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.
whoa.tryLine: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.

whoa.headline: She built a flashlight that runs on body heat
whoa.summary: Ann Makosinski was 15. She made a hollow flashlight with no batteries - just the heat from your hand. It won a big science fair and actually worked.
whoa.try: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.

whoa.headline: A lock is just a bunch of tiny lifts
whoa.summary: Your key is a row of hills. Each hill lifts a pin to the exact right height so the cylinder can turn. Wrong key = one pin still blocking.
whoa.try: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.
whoa.tryLine: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.

whoa.headline: The 60-second room reset
whoa.summary: Set a timer. Clothes on the chair, rubbish in the bin, stuff you used back where it lives. Don't clean. Just reset. Most rooms look 80% better in one minute.
whoa.try: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.
whoa.tryLine: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.

whoa.headline: Someone laughs at your idea
whoa.summary: Don't laugh at yourself to join in. Try: "Okay, but I'm still going to try it." Short. Calm. You didn't attack them, and you didn't drop the idea.
whoa.try: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.

whoa.headline: Your brain dumps the mission mid-walk
whoa.summary: You stand up, walk into a room, and forget why. Doorways actually reset a bit of your memory. Your brain files "kitchen plan" and starts "hallway plan."
whoa.try: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.
whoa.tryLine: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.

whoa.headline: "Look up at the stars and not down at your feet."
whoa.summary: Stephen Hawking said that. He meant: spend your brain on big, interesting things, not on small worries. You can do both in one night - homework, then 2 minutes of sky.
whoa.try: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.
whoa.tryLine: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.

whoa.headline: Tardigrades can survive outer space
whoa.summary: These tiny "water bears" can dry out, freeze, and even go into space with no suit - then wake up later and walk around. They are almost impossible to kill.
whoa.try: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.
whoa.tryLine: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.

whoa.headline: At 13 he built a radio station from junk
whoa.summary: Kelvin Doe lived in Sierra Leone with almost no money for parts. He made batteries from acid, soda and metal, then a transmitter from scrap. Neighbours tuned in to his station for music and local news. MIT later invited him to show how he did it.
whoa.try: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?
whoa.tryLine: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?

whoa.headline: The game already started without you
whoa.summary: Don't hover. Walk up and say "Got room for one more?" If they say not this round: "Cool, I'll jump in next." Then watch like a teammate, not like a sad statue.
whoa.try: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.
whoa.tryLine: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.

whoa.headline: Wi - Fi is just shouted numbers, very fast
whoa.summary: Your router yells invisible radio blips. Your phone listens and turns the blips back into pictures and words. Walls eat some of the yell, which is why the signal dies in the bathroom.
whoa.try: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.
whoa.tryLine: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.

whoa.headline: Cows pick a best friend - and stay calmer together
whoa.summary: Scientists found many cows choose one favourite cow and hang out with them. Smart farms keep those pairs together, because friend-cows eat better and stay healthier. Even cows know a good teammate helps.
whoa.try: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.
whoa.tryLine: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.

whoa.headline: Remember any name with one trick
whoa.summary: When you meet someone, say their name back once: "Cool, I'm ___, hi Maya." Then stick it to a picture in your head - Maya with a map. People light up when you get it right next time.
whoa.try: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.

whoa.headline: There are more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy
whoa.summary: The Milky Way has around 100 billion stars. Earth has about 3 trillion trees. We still cut them down too fast - but the planet is greener and stranger than it looks from a car.
whoa.try: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.
whoa.tryLine: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.

whoa.headline: Hunt: one free kids thing this week
whoa.summary: Libraries, museums and parks quietly run free drop-ins. Pick one, show up, stay 20 minutes. That counts as an adventure.
whoa.try: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.
whoa.tryLine: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.

whoa.headline: JWST reveals a race against time for forming planets
whoa.summary: Planets form from disks of gas and dust around young stars, but the gas needed for growth does not last forever. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now offer a new view of how this gas escapes and how the process changes as young planetary systems develop.

whoa.headline: SpaceX announces plans for $100 billion 'spaceport' in Louisiana
whoa.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX announced plans Tuesday to build a $100 billion facility in the southern U.S. state of Louisiana to launch its anticipated Starship megarockets, currently being developed at the company's Texas Starbase.

whoa.headline: Astronauts Anil Menon and Sophie Adenot on Spacewalk
whoa.summary: From left, Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA (partially obscured and wearing the spacesuit with a red stripe on the legs) and Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) work together during a six - hour and 23 - minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station.

whoa.headline: Cutting-edge infrared space telescope Roman set to launch
whoa.summary: The NASA-led Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch on 30 August 2026 at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST / 13:26 CEST from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA. With its wide field of view and advanced optical design, the Roman telescope will conduct detailed scans of the sky in visible to near-infrared light. In doing so, Roman will help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter and find new exoplanets.

whoa.headline: Legendary rugby league player Billy Boston dies aged 92
whoa.summary: Billy Boston, the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood, has passed away at the age of 92.

whoa.headline: Africa's Wild Dogs Are the Most Hated Carnivores on the Continent. Here's How Some Conservationists Are Saving Them Anyway.
whoa.summary: Meet the team that closely monitors the playful canines, who need help to form diverse packs and stop their numbers from dwindling

whoa.headline: Frozen poop reveals Ice Age squirrels' ecosystem
whoa.summary: Frozen, ice-age squirrel poop doesn't stink. At least not at first. But that changes if it warms.

whoa.headline: A casting spell brings Kit Harington to Hogwarts as its newest teacher
whoa.summary: Kit Harington will replace Nicholas Hoult as Hogwarts teacher Gilderoy Lockhart in the second season of the highly anticipated Harry Potter HBO TV series.

whoa.headline: Millions of 10p coins with King on enter circulation
whoa.summary: Royal Mint releases new 10p coins with the King's portrait into banks and post offices.

whoa.headline: NASA starshade would enable astronomers to directly image rocky exoworlds
whoa.summary: A NASA-led team hopes to take a shortcut to direct imaging of extrasolar Earth-like planets. The idea is to use what they call a hybrid telescope composed of an orbital starshade coupled with the next-generation extremely large ground-based optical telescopes.

whoa.headline: Meteorite dust holds records of magnetism that may have helped form the sun
whoa.summary: Around 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system was little more than a giant ball of gas and dust. Over the next few million years, this "solar nebula" underwent a huge transformation, flattening into a disk of matter that then condensed to form the central sun and orbiting planets.

whoa.headline: NASA Astronaut Reid Wiseman at Freedom 250 Grand Prix
whoa.summary: NASA astronaut Reid Wiseman, Artemis II commander, is seen in the two-seat IndyCar as he prepares for driver Conor Daly to take him on a lap in the fastest seat in sport ahead of the start of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Photo Credit: (NASA/Joel Kowsky)

whoa.headline: Why did this football cost £2.5 million?
whoa.summary: Maradona's infamous 'Hand of God' football sells for millions. We take a look at why it's so expensive!

whoa.headline: Scientists Say: Midden
whoa.summary: Midden (noun, "MID-den") A midden is a garbage pile or dump site left by ancient people. This word also describes a pile of items gathered by an animal. Old trash heaps can contain artifacts of ancient life.

whoa.headline: Art helped this astrophysicist make sense of math
whoa.summary: When Ronald Gamble first learned about black holes as a teen, he read as much as he could about them. But he noticed that researchers still had much to learn about how they worked. "The mystery of black holes really drove me to study them," he says.

whoa.headline: China says unmanned moon mission delayed over 'launch conditions'
whoa.summary: China's manned space agency said Sunday it is delaying a research moon mission that is part of Beijing's efforts to land a crew there by 2030, less than two weeks after a rare launch failure.

whoa.headline: Hair We Go! Haaland loses goal-den locks for start of the season
whoa.summary: Hair today, gone tomorrow! Haaland unveils a short new look before City's season opener and gets mixed reactions from friends.

whoa.headline: Happy News: Stories to make you smile
whoa.summary: De-Graft brings us this week's Happy News. There are unusual, furry friends, colourful kites and some social media stars.

whoa.headline: JWST peeks at Callisto's ancient scars
whoa.summary: Of Jupiter's four Galilean moons, Callisto is the one that gets the least attention. Io is constantly being resurfaced by volcanoes. Europa has a giant liquid water ocean.

whoa.headline: Webb Opens Treasure Chest
whoa.summary: This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month takes us to a fantastical realm within our home galaxy, where piercing starlight and billowing winds sculpt dust clouds into inventive shapes. This scene is from the Carina Nebula, which lies just 7500 light-years away in the constellation Carina (the Keel).

whoa.headline: Stellar eruptions in the laboratory: First experimental evidence for their suppression in strong magnetic fields
whoa.summary: An international team of astrophysicists and plasma physicists has provided the first experimental evidence that strong magnetic fields surrounding active stars can completely suppress coronal mass ejections. This offers clues to why massive stellar eruptions are rarely observed on stars other than the sun.

whoa.headline: Stellar spin may explain why repeated black hole flares grow dimmer
whoa.summary: At the center of most galaxies lies a supermassive black hole, with a mass millions to billions of times that of our sun and some of the most extreme gravity in the universe.

whoa.headline: China to launch robotic mission to the Moon
whoa.summary: The Chang'e-7 mission will see the exploration of the Moon's south pole in search of water ice.

whoa.headline: What is El Niño and how could it affect our weather?
whoa.summary: What is El Niño, and how can warmer Pacific Ocean water change winds, rainfall and temperatures in the UK and across the world?

whoa.headline: Humans have used fire far longer than anyone realized
whoa.summary: A cave in Africa seems to host the oldest known traces of humans using fire. Burnt remnants of animal bones hint that groups of Homo erectus used fires here as long as 1.8 million years ago. The site is known as Wonderwerk Cave.

whoa.headline: Strange News: The weirdest stories of the week
whoa.summary: De-Graft has your weekly portion of Strange News. There are goats on a bus, robots on a football pitch and an enormous omelette in a gigantic pan.

whoa.headline: Quiz of the Week: Have you been following this week's news?
whoa.summary: It's been a busy week of big stories and headlines. Have you been keeping up with the news over the last seven days? Test your knowledge of the latest top stories with our Quiz of the Week.

whoa.headline: Japan to launch probe for Mars moons in October: Space agency
whoa.summary: Japan's ambitious mission to collect and bring back samples from one of Mars' moons will lift off Oct. 20, the space agency announced Thursday.

whoa.headline: Artemis Mission Patches
whoa.summary: A NASA jacket containing Artemis I and II mission patches, along with other NASA patches hangs on the back of a chair on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026, inside Firing Room 1 of the Rocco A. Petrone Launch Control Center at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida during a terminal countdown simulation for the Artemis III mission.

whoa.headline: Interstellar travel IV: Solar, magnetic, & directed-energy sails
whoa.summary: Welcome back to our series on interstellar travel! In our first installment, we examined attempts to realize nuclear propulsion and how the technology could be used to reach the nearest star. In our second, we examined how fusion power has also been considered a means of propelling spacecraft to relativistic speeds (a fraction of the speed of light).

whoa.headline: Rising sea temperatures changing how whales hunt
whoa.summary: Hundreds of the world's biggest whales including humpbacks, minke and fin whales have taken advantage of rising sea temperatures in East Greenland.

whoa.headline: How to lessen your pet's impacts on the planet
whoa.summary: While John Harvey was working as a veterinarian in Devon, England, his clinic looked for ways to lower its carbon footprint . They installed energy-efficient light bulbs. This got Harvey thinking: What about the animals?

whoa.headline: Prince Harry and family moving back to UK
whoa.summary: Prince Harry, his wife Meghan and their two children, have been living in the United States but now their children will be starting a British school in September.

whoa.headline: Thousands of teenagers getting their GCSE results
whoa.summary: If you have older siblings, family or friends getting their important exam results, it's a very big day. Be nice and prepare for nerves!

whoa.headline: Racing to build a radio telescope on the moon
whoa.summary: Remember the "Wow!" signal? That high-energy radio signature occurred in 1977, when Earth was much "quieter" in the radio band. If it happened today, it probably wouldn't even move the needle on the background noise of human radio chatter.

whoa.headline: Dark Stars may have left gravitational-wave echoes across the universe
whoa.summary: A mysterious background of extremely low-frequency gravitational waves detected by networks of pulsars may carry information about events that began more than 13 billion years ago - including the formation of some of the first supermassive black holes in the universe.

whoa.headline: Ancient Milky Way Merger
whoa.summary: About 12 billion years ago, a dwarf galaxy known as LKH collided with a young Milky Way and merged with it. This artist's concept portrays that collision. NASA's Hubble Space Telescope uncovered definitive evidence of this collision by studying globular star clusters.

whoa.headline: Nasa reveal photos of Moon crater after SpaceX rocket crash
whoa.summary: Scientists estimate the crater is around 18 metres in width and about three metres deep. Find out more here.

whoa.headline: Man City's World Cup winner Rodri joins Barcelona
whoa.summary: The superstar midfielder Rodri, who was voted the best player at the World Cup, is heading back to Spain.

whoa.headline: AI can be a helpful math tutor if used right - and harmful if not
whoa.summary: Is it a good idea to use artificial intelligence (AI) for math help? Yes - and no. That's based on the results of a new survey.

whoa.headline: Fly around Schiaparelli Crater with Mars Express
whoa.summary: Video: 00:04:10 ESA's Mars Express takes us on another mesmerising flight, this time around one of the biggest craters on Mars. Despite measuring a huge 460 km across, Schiaparelli Crater seems to be relatively shallow. Perhaps it has been filled in over the last few billion years by sediment blown by the wind or deposited by water, by lava - or by a combination of all three.

whoa.headline: Cleaner air may help children's lungs grow, study suggests
whoa.summary: Researchers looked at a the health of primary school pupils living in London before and after pollution restrictions were introduced. Find out more here.

whoa.headline: Mars attacks: How much dust from the red planet is safe to breathe?
whoa.summary: NASA has released a report recommending an initial health standard for the Martian dust that astronauts could inhale during future missions. Although sending people to Mars is still years away, NASA needs to establish safety limits now. Spacecraft, spacesuits and crew habitats take years to design and test, and engineers need a measurable target for developing air filters, airlocks and suit-cleaning systems that will keep astronauts safe.

whoa.headline: Dying radio galaxies suggest a shorter, more dynamic afterlife for black hole jets
whoa.summary: Astronomers have uncovered a previously underexplored population of faint, rapidly fading remnant radio galaxies, offering new insights into what happens after supermassive black holes stop powering their enormous radio jets.

whoa.headline: Earth's Organisms Developed Via Evolution. Some Theorists Wonder: What if the Entire Cosmos Did, Too?
whoa.summary: The idea that universes evolve like organisms sat on the fringes of theoretical physics for decades. Then, a Substack post and a 2022 find by the James Webb Space Telescope boosted the concept

whoa.headline: NASA's B777 Gets New Coat of Paint
whoa.summary: NASA's Boeing 777 returns to the agency's Langley Research Center after receiving a new paint scheme.

whoa.headline: Ruby-forming mineral found by Mars rover hints at violent impacts
whoa.summary: So far, most of the minerals found on Mars tell a story of lava poured out by ancient volcanoes, followed by long stretches in which water trickled through and slowly reshaped the rock. However, some rocks scattered across the Martian surface seem to hint at a different geological history - carrying the same material that forms rubies and sapphires.

wins.headline: The ozone hole is shrinking
wins.summary: Countries banned the chemicals that were eating the sky's sunscreen. Scientists now measure the hole getting smaller. A giant problem, slowly reversing.
wins.try: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.
wins.tryLine: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.

wins.headline: Humpback whales came back from the brink
wins.summary: Hunting nearly wiped them out. Bans and watchers gave them decades of quiet. Many populations have rebounded enough that boats now have to share the water.
wins.try: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.
wins.tryLine: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.

wins.headline: Kids' blood lead levels crashed
wins.summary: Lead in petrol and paint used to quietly hurt brains. Laws pulled it out. Average levels in many countries fell hard. Policy can be a superpower.
wins.try: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.
wins.tryLine: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.

wins.headline: Humans wiped one killer disease off Earth
wins.summary: Smallpox used to scar and kill millions. Vaccines plus a worldwide hunt ended it in 1980. It is the only human disease we have fully erased.
wins.try: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.
wins.tryLine: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.

wins.headline: Some rivers got otters back
wins.summary: Cleaner water and protection let otters return to rivers that were empty. If you see one, that's a report card for the whole valley.
wins.try: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.
wins.tryLine: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.

wins.headline: Solar got cheap enough to flood the grid
wins.summary: Panels used to be a rich-country toy. Prices crashed. Now whole countries add solar faster than coal. The physics did not change. The cost did.
wins.try: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.
wins.tryLine: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.

wins.headline: Kids ran a little free library street
wins.summary: A box on a lawn. Take a book, leave a book. Some streets now have three. No app, no fee, just neighbours trusting kids with stories.
wins.try: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.
wins.tryLine: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.

wins.headline: Some coral is being grown in nurseries
wins.summary: Divers farm hardy coral and glue it back onto damaged reef. Not a full fix. It is a start, and fish move back in.
wins.try: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.
wins.tryLine: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.

wins.headline: Cities that built bike lanes got more bikes
wins.summary: Paint and kerbs changed who dared to ride. Kids included. Safer paths, more riders, fewer cars on short trips. Design beats nagging.
wins.try: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.
wins.tryLine: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.

wins.headline: Bag charges slashed plastic at the till
wins.summary: A few pence changed habits faster than posters. Many countries saw single-use bags crash. Small price, huge pile of plastic not made.
wins.try: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.
wins.tryLine: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.

wins.headline: A teen built a cheaper hearing test
wins.summary: Julian Wilson and others have built simple phone-based hearing checks so more kids get spotted early. Not a hospital. A screen and a plan.
wins.try: If someone talks loud at you a lot, a hearing check is kindness, not teasing.
wins.tryLine: If someone talks loud at you a lot, a hearing check is kindness, not teasing.

wins.headline: Beavers got invited back on purpose
wins.summary: They build wetlands that soak floods and help fish. Some rivers that were ditches now hold water again. A rodent as infrastructure.
wins.try: Look up a beaver dam photo. That's a living dam.
wins.tryLine: Look up a beaver dam photo. That's a living dam.

wins.headline: Dark-sky towns switched the lights down
wins.summary: Warmer, downward lamps cut glare. Stars came back. Turtles and owls got a quieter night. You can still see the pavement.
wins.try: On a clear night, count stars in one window of sky.
wins.tryLine: On a clear night, count stars in one window of sky.

wins.headline: Kids redesigned their own playground
wins.summary: Some schools asked pupils to map the boring bits, then rebuild. More climbing, more shade, fewer 'don't'. Behaviour got better because the place got better.

harvest.headline: Cutting-edge infrared space telescope Roman set to launch
harvest.summary: The NASA-led Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is set to launch on 30 August 2026 at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST / 13:26 CEST from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA. With its wide field of view and advanced optical design, the Roman telescope will conduct detailed scans of the sky in visible to near-infrared light. In doing so, Roman will help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter and find new exoplanets.

harvest.headline: Africa's Wild Dogs Are the Most Hated Carnivores on the Continent. Here's How Some Conservationists Are Saving Them Anyway.
harvest.summary: Meet the team that closely monitors the playful canines, who need help to form diverse packs and stop their numbers from dwindling

harvest.headline: Frozen poop reveals Ice Age squirrels' ecosystem
harvest.summary: Frozen, ice-age squirrel poop doesn't stink. At least not at first. But that changes if it warms.

harvest.headline: Scientists Say: Midden
harvest.summary: Midden (noun, "MID-den") A midden is a garbage pile or dump site left by ancient people. This word also describes a pile of items gathered by an animal. Old trash heaps can contain artifacts of ancient life.

harvest.headline: Art helped this astrophysicist make sense of math
harvest.summary: When Ronald Gamble first learned about black holes as a teen, he read as much as he could about them. But he noticed that researchers still had much to learn about how they worked. "The mystery of black holes really drove me to study them," he says.

harvest.headline: Fly around Schiaparelli Crater with Mars Express
harvest.summary: Video: 00:04:10 ESA's Mars Express takes us on another mesmerising flight, this time around one of the biggest craters on Mars. Despite measuring a huge 460 km across, Schiaparelli Crater seems to be relatively shallow. Perhaps it has been filled in over the last few billion years by sediment blown by the wind or deposited by water, by lava - or by a combination of all three.

harvest.headline: Earth's Organisms Developed Via Evolution. Some Theorists Wonder: What if the Entire Cosmos Did, Too?
harvest.summary: The idea that universes evolve like organisms sat on the fringes of theoretical physics for decades. Then, a Substack post and a 2022 find by the James Webb Space Telescope boosted the concept

harvest.headline: Hubble & Gaia solve our galaxy's merger mystery
harvest.summary: Our home galaxy, the Milky Way, grew to its current size in part by consuming smaller galaxies. Now, new data from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope show definitive evidence of a dwarf galaxy merging with the young Milky Way galaxy in the earliest phases of its evolution. This finding extends our knowledge of our galaxy's history 1.8 billion years farther back in time than before.

harvest.headline: Marine Biologists Solved a Wildlife Mystery From the Walkway of the Golden Gate Bridge: How the Harbor Porpoise Mates
harvest.summary: The dolphin-like marine mammals returned to San Francisco Bay in 2008 after a decades-long absence from the area. Scientists took the rare opportunity to closely observe their behavior, and what they uncovered might help at-risk porpoise populations

harvest.headline: NGC 7380: The Wizard Nebula
harvest.summary: What powers are being wielded in the Wizard Nebula? Gravitation strong enough to form stars, and stellar winds and radiations powerful enough to create and dissolve towers of gas. Located only 8,000 light years away, the Wizard nebula, featured here, surrounds a developing open star cluster NGC 7380. harvest.summary: How close will Jupiter and Saturn be at their Great Conjunction? Consider this beautiful triple conjunction of Moon, Jupiter and Saturn captured through clouds in the wintry twilight. The telephoto view looks toward the western horizon and the Alborz Mountains in Iran after sunset on December 17. harvest.headline: JWST reveals a race against time for forming planets
harvest.summary: Planets form from disks of gas and dust around young stars, but the gas needed for growth does not last forever. New observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) now offer a new view of how this gas escapes and how the process changes as young planetary systems develop.

harvest.headline: SpaceX announces plans for $100 billion 'spaceport' in Louisiana
harvest.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX announced plans Tuesday to build a $100 billion facility in the southern U.S. state of Louisiana to launch its anticipated Starship megarockets, currently being developed at the company's Texas Starbase.

harvest.headline: Astronauts Anil Menon and Sophie Adenot on Spacewalk
harvest.summary: From left, Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA (partially obscured and wearing the spacesuit with a red stripe on the legs) and Sophie Adenot of ESA (European Space Agency) work together during a six - hour and 23 - minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station.

harvest.headline: Legendary rugby league player Billy Boston dies aged 92
harvest.summary: Billy Boston, the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood, has passed away at the age of 92.

harvest.summary: Kit Harington will replace Nicholas Hoult as Hogwarts teacher Gilderoy Lockhart in the second season of the highly anticipated Harry Potter HBO TV series.

harvest.headline: Webb Opens Treasure Chest
harvest.summary: This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month takes us to a fantastical realm within our home galaxy, where piercing starlight and billowing winds sculpt dust clouds into inventive shapes. This scene is from the Carina Nebula, which lies just 7500 light-years away in the constellation Carina (the Keel).
